title: Low mood, visual hallucinations, and falls – heralding the onset of rapidly progressive probable sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease in a 73-year old: a case report
case_prompt:
A 73-year-old previously well and independent woman was brought to the emergency department with a 2-week history of worsening confusion and new behavioral changes. Her family described vivid visual hallucinations, including seeing men around her bed and searching for her deceased sister. Two weeks prior, she experienced vertigo and a fall without head trauma. She had a history of hypertension, depression, and anxiety, and had recently restarted paroxetine. She took prochlorperazine and doxazosin, denied alcohol or illicit drug use, and had no infective symptoms.

On examination, she was alert (GCS 15), scored 9/10 on the Abbreviated Mental Test, and had blood pressure 160/63 mmHg. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams were normal. Neurologically, she had a wide-based gait, veered left on standing, brisk lower-limb reflexes (left>right), left-sided intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesis, and past‐pointing—consistent with a predominantly cerebellar syndrome with some upper motor neuron signs.

Initial blood tests showed CRP 9.8 mg/L (0–7.9), urea 9.0 mmol/L (2.8–7.2), and otherwise normal FBC, U&E, bone profile, LFTs, and TFTs. Urine dipstick was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Brain MRI reported a few small nonspecific white matter lesions with no intracranial abnormality correlating with her symptoms; no comment was made on the thalamus or basal ganglia.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infection — “Frequent causes of confusion in the elderly – infection... – were all investigated with blood tests and scans and a psychiatry opinion sought…”  
2. Drug or alcohol intoxication or withdrawal — “Frequent causes of confusion in the elderly – infection, drug/alcohol intoxication or withdrawal…– were all investigated with blood tests and scans…”  
3. Metabolic disturbances — “Frequent causes of confusion in the elderly –… metabolic…– were all investigated with blood tests and scans…”  
4. Vascular events — “Frequent causes of confusion in the elderly –… vascular – were all investigated with blood tests and scans…”  
5. Depression — “a psychiatry opinion sought relating to her known diagnosis of depression.”  
6. Alcohol use causing cerebellar symptoms — “Common causes of cerebellar symptoms – alcohol use, vascular – were appropriately investigated. However, our patient’s family did not report an alcohol history…”  
7. Vascular cerebellar causes — “Common causes of cerebellar symptoms – alcohol use, vascular – were appropriately investigated.”  
8. Herpes simplex encephalitis — “Following admission, she was started empirically on acyclovir for herpes simplex encephalitis... the CSF did not support this diagnosis.”  
9. Viral encephalitis — “EEG showed... interrupted by prolonged runs of... triphasic waves... possible causes including prion disease, viral encephalitis, metabolic, and vascular.”  
10. Prion disease — “With EEG and specialist interpretation of the MRI, CJD was the most likely diagnosis to account for all of her symptoms… Probable diagnosis of sCJD was further confirmed with supporting CSF findings: positive for 14–3-3 protein, raised protein levels of s-100b > 2.5 ng/mL… and a positive RT-QuIC.”
